title: How to Tell Wild Animals
subject: English

notes.heading: Word Meanings
points: Advance: To walk directly towards or move forward.
Tawny: Having a yellowish-brown or brownish-yellow skin colour.
Discern: To recognize, identify, or distinguish with difficulty.
Roaming: Wandering or walking around casually.
Noble: Having a grand, majestic, or royal appearance.
Ground: The background surface or main colour of an animal's hide.
Strolling forth: Walking forward slowly and casually.
Hide: The thick skin of an animal.
Peppered: Covered or spread thickly with tiny spots.
Lept (Leapt): Jumped or pounced forward forcefully.
Yard: The backyard or lawn area surrounding a house.
Caress: A gentle, loving touch or hug (used ironically here).
Distinguish: To recognize the clear differences between two things.
Beasts of prey: Dangerous wild animals that hunt other animals for food.
Novice: A person who is completely new or inexperienced at a job.
Nonplus: To be completely surprised, puzzled, or confused.
Weep: To shed tears or cry uncontrollably.
Chameleon: A small, lizard-like reptile capable of changing its skin colour to camouflage.

summary: "How to Tell Wild Animals" by Carolyn Wells is a humorous and lighthearted poem that provides readers with a series of witty, unconventional, and dangerous strategies for identifying various wild beasts in the jungle. The poet uses a playful tone to explain that if you happen to go to the jungles in the east, you can identify the large, tawny Asian Lion by its terrifying roar that makes you feel as though you are dying of fright. If a noble wild beast with black stripes on a yellow coat greets you and eats you up, you can be certain it is the majestic Bengal Tiger. Moving further, a beast whose hide is covered with spots and who leaps upon you repeatedly can be recognized as the  Leopard, as no amount of roaring with pain will save you from its continuous pouncing. If you are walking around your yard and meet a creature that hugs you very hard, you are dealing with a Bear, whose tight embrace is a surefire sign of its identity. The poet also draws a distinct line between a Hyena and a Crocodile, noting that a hyena will always approach you with a deceptive, merry smile, whereas a crocodile will weep fake tears while devouring its prey. Finally, the poem introduces the Chameleon, a small, lizard-like creature that has no ears or wings, explaining that if you look at a tree and see absolutely nothing there, it is because the camouflaged chameleon is sitting on the branch, proving that nature is full of wondrous and deceptive surprises.

qa.q: Does ‘dyin’ really rhyme with ‘lion’? Can you say it in the same way as ‘lion’?
qa.a: ​ No, “dyin’” does not exactly rhyme with “lion” in the usual pronunciation. The poet uses it as a humorous rhyme with “lion” to make the poem playful and funny.

qa.q: How does the poet suggest that you identify the lion and the tiger?
qa.a: ​ The poet humorously suggests that if a large animal approaches you in the jungle and roars while attacking you, it is a lion. If it has black stripes and kills you suddenly, it is a tiger.

qa.q: What is the theme of the poem?
qa.a: ​ The poem humorously describes how to identify different wild animals. It uses exaggeration, rhyme and irony to make the descriptions funny and entertaining.

qa.q: Why does the poet use humour in the poem?
qa.a: ​ The poet uses humour to make the poem enjoyable and memorable. The dangerous nature of wild animals is presented in a funny way, making the poem light-hearted rather than frightening.

qa.q: How does the poet describe the bear?
qa.a: ​ The poet says that a bear can be identified when it hugs you tightly. The humorous description suggests that its hug would actually be dangerous because the bear might crush the person.
